claims: Start position and timing trigger materially affect measured sprint-start performance.
{{canonicalName}} must record its start constraint separately from sprint distance and timing method.
The start, push-off, and first acceleration steps are related but distinguishable parts of short sprint acceleration.
{{canonicalName}} belongs to linear locomotion and acceleration output; stance, cue, and distance remain controlled variant dimensions.
Sprint acceleration requires rapid lower-limb force production and coordinated hip, knee, and ankle action.
Hamstring function contributes to horizontally oriented force production during acceleration.
Early acceleration performance is associated with forward-directed impulse, propulsive force, and progressive projection through the first steps.
One universal setup or forced first-step geometry is not appropriate across different bodies and start constraints.
Standing, three-point, and block starts produce different timing and body-position effects.
Difficulty scoring must include start complexity, coordination, supervision, impact, and failure consequence rather than treating all unloaded starts as difficulty 40.
Power output is highest during the first steps of sprint acceleration.
The card should track neural intent, high-speed lower-limb contacts, local posterior-chain stress, technical fatigue sensitivity, and performance recovery.
Quality sprint work needs a suitable surface, marked start and finish, sufficient run-out, and recovery that preserves the intended speed quality.
Start setup, footwear, lane separation, athlete readiness, and coach sightline are relevant constraints for {{canonicalName}}.
Acceleration sessions should prescribe distance, intensity, repetitions, sets, and recovery rather than repetitions alone.
Recovery and total volume should preserve fast, technically consistent efforts instead of converting start work into conditioning.
The setup should support rapid hip extension and forward propulsion without forcing an anthropometrically inappropriate position.
Athletes should project, push the ground backward, coordinate arm action, accelerate through the target, and use the planned run-out.
Youth training should use qualified supervision, correct technique, manageable demands, and gradual progression.
Stop for pain, limping, repeated stumble, unsafe spacing or surface, loss of posture, or visible speed decline that does not recover with rest.
Acceleration and maximal-velocity sprinting are distinct training qualities.
{{canonicalName}} should be placed fresh in output or skill work; dense submaximal conditioning requires a separate delivery profile.
Acceleration develops incrementally across successive steps rather than by immediately standing upright.
Athlete-facing support should use one or two task cues, define a successful start and finish, and avoid prescribing identical stride shapes to every athlete.
Coaches should distinguish the target acceleration quality from maximal velocity and conditioning.
Observation should include setup consistency, projection, force direction, arm-leg coordination, split performance where available, and safe completion.
Speed work should be developmentally appropriate and based on movement competency.
Distance, intent, start complexity, cue complexity, rest, and timing pressure can be scaled while retaining a short-acceleration learning objective.
Start position and timing procedure change the task and measured performance.
Stance and cue changes should usually be modeled as variants; small distance changes are dosage annotations, while a flying start changes the primary stimulus to maximal velocity.
YouTube supports privacy-enhanced embedding through youtube-nocookie.com.
The candidates for {{canonicalName}} returned current oEmbed player responses, but exact-version, full-content, caption, safety, and demonstration-quality review remain human gates.

assessmentSummary.identity: A short maximal or near-maximal acceleration effort beginning from a two-point standing or staggered stance.
currentCardFindings: The card has empty controlled taxonomy, anatomy, equipment, environment, population, load, and fatigue fields.
Uniform 40 difficulty values understate coordination, supervision, impact, and failure consequence and omit required score dimensions.
The generic description spans many sports but does not define distance, start geometry, run-out, dosage, or observable quality.
assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Retain as a two-point start variant of short acceleration. Prescribe 5–20 m, full run-out, high intent, and enough recovery to keep split time and projection stable.

alternateAssessments.name: 3-Point Acceleration Start
alternateAssessments.rationale: Adding one hand to the ground changes setup and initial projection but retains short acceleration as the primary stimulus.

alternateAssessments.name: Falling Acceleration Start
alternateAssessments.rationale: A forward fall constrains projection and initiation without changing the central acceleration identity.

alternateAssessments.name: Block Start
alternateAssessments.rationale: Starting blocks change equipment, setup, and push-off mechanics while remaining a sprint-start variant.

alternateAssessments.name: 2-Point Start 20m
alternateAssessments.rationale: Distance is dosage metadata when stance, intent, and primary acceleration stimulus are unchanged.

assessmentSummary.identity: A 10–20 m short acceleration from a three-point stance with one hand grounded.
currentCardFindings: The card lacks controlled taxonomy, anatomy, constraints, load, fatigue, and complete difficulty dimensions.
Its four difficulty values are identical to simpler standing starts even though setup and transition demands are higher.
Distance is embedded in the name but should remain an explicit dosage range rather than a separate identity.
assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Model as a three-point short-acceleration variant. Preserve setup consistency and forward projection; treat 10 versus 20 m as dosage and keep recovery long enough for maximal-quality efforts.

alternateAssessments.name: 2-Point Start 10–20m
alternateAssessments.rationale: Removing the ground hand simplifies setup while retaining short acceleration.

alternateAssessments.name: Four-Point Start 10–20m
alternateAssessments.rationale: A four-point setup changes support and transition mechanics but retains the primary acceleration task.

alternateAssessments.name: Block Start 10–20m
alternateAssessments.rationale: Blocks materially change equipment and push-off conditions but belong to the same sprint-start family.

alternateAssessments.name: 3-Point Start 10 Yards
alternateAssessments.rationale: A small distance and measurement-system change is dosage metadata, not a new movement identity.

assessmentSummary.identity: A short acceleration initiated by a controlled forward fall from standing, followed by a forceful first step and continued acceleration through 10 m.
currentCardFindings: The card lacks controlled taxonomy, constraints, load, fatigue, and complete difficulty scoring.
The forward-fall constraint adds balance, timing, and failure-consequence demands that are not represented by uniform 40 scores.
Several existing falling-start names appear semantically identical or differ only by 10 m versus 10 yards.
assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Treat the forward fall as a start variant and 10 m as dosage. Require a controlled whole-body fall, timely recovery step, clear lane, and full run-out; regress to a two-point start if the athlete reaches or stumbles.

alternateAssessments.name: Falling Start Sprint
alternateAssessments.rationale: The unspecified-distance name describes the same controlled-fall acceleration task and should resolve to one identity with distance in dosage.

alternateAssessments.name: Falling Start to 10 Meters
alternateAssessments.rationale: This is a spelling-level expression of the exact same start constraint and distance.

alternateAssessments.name: Falling Start to 10 Yards
alternateAssessments.rationale: The small distance and unit change is dosage metadata when execution and intent remain unchanged.

alternateAssessments.name: Band-Resisted Falling Start
alternateAssessments.rationale: External resistance changes equipment and force-velocity demand while retaining the falling-start constraint.

assessmentSummary.identity: A 5–10 yard acceleration initiated from a stable half-kneeling stance, transitioning through the front foot into sprinting.
currentCardFindings: The description is specific, but all controlled taxonomy, anatomy, constraints, load, fatigue, and most difficulty dimensions are empty.
Rising from the floor increases transition coordination, mobility, and supervision demands beyond a standing start.
The card does not identify kneeling-surface comfort, lead-leg symmetry, hand position, or safe transition criteria.
assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Retain as a start-position variant used for first-step projection and floor-to-sprint transition. Dose both lead legs, provide knee-friendly support when needed, and regress if the athlete pushes from the rear knee or loses balance.

alternateAssessments.name: Tall-Kneeling Start Sprint
alternateAssessments.rationale: Starting with both knees down changes the transition and available front-foot contribution while retaining floor-to-sprint acceleration.

alternateAssessments.name: Prone Start Sprint
alternateAssessments.rationale: A prone start adds a larger floor transition and different upper-body contribution.

alternateAssessments.name: Half-Kneeling Start 5 Yards
alternateAssessments.rationale: Distance is dosage metadata within the same half-kneeling start task.

alternateAssessments.name: Half-Kneeling Start with Auditory Cue
alternateAssessments.rationale: An unpredictable external go-signal adds simple-reaction demand to the same physical start.

assessmentSummary.identity: A short sprint acceleration initiated in response to an unpredictable, standardized auditory go-signal.
currentCardFindings: The generic explosiveness description does not define cue type, cue intensity, waiting interval, start stance, sprint distance, or false-start handling.
The current 40 scores omit reaction and anticipation-control demands, supervision, failure consequence, and impact.
Several current media candidates are general start or agility videos and require exact auditory-start visual review.
assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Use a consistent non-startling cue, randomized wait, one prepared response, and a clear lane. Measure reaction separately from acceleration where possible; reject anticipated starts and stop before cue discrimination or sprint mechanics decline.

claims: An auditory sprint start includes a measurable reaction interval between the go-signal and force or movement onset.
{{canonicalName}} requires an unpredictable auditory cue and a pre-declared sprint response; a self-selected start is a different task.
Auditory reaction time contains neural and neuromuscular components in addition to physical sprint-start execution.
Difficulty should include cue attention and anticipation control alongside the physical start and acceleration demands.
Simple auditory reaction is a specific cue-response task.
Cue modality is a variant dimension; adding directional choice changes the decision task and should not be silently merged with simple reaction.

alternateAssessments.name: Whistle Start Sprint
alternateAssessments.rationale: A whistle is an implementation of the same auditory go-signal when intensity and predictability are controlled.

alternateAssessments.name: Visual-Cue Start Sprint
alternateAssessments.rationale: Changing cue modality changes sensory processing while preserving the prepared sprint response.

alternateAssessments.name: Self-Selected Start Sprint
alternateAssessments.rationale: Removing the external go-signal removes reaction time and anticipation control from the primary task.

alternateAssessments.name: Auditory Choice-Direction Sprint
alternateAssessments.rationale: Mapping different sounds to different directions adds choice reaction and decision accuracy, materially changing the task.

alternateAssessments.name: Randomized Wait Auditory Start
alternateAssessments.rationale: Varying the ready-to-go interval is a cue-timing dosage parameter within the same simple auditory reaction task.
